FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard [P : 54] (Third Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards after the draft 
finalized by the Methods of Measurement and Test for Petroleum, Petroleum Products and Lubricants Sectional 
Committee had been approved by the Petroleum, Coal and Related Products Division Council. 


This standard was first published in 1960 and subsequently revised in 1979 and 2007. Second revision of this 
standard was identical with ISO 4265 : 1986. After withdrawal of ISO Standard, the Sectional Committee decided 
to revise the Indian Standard to remove dual numbering. 


In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, is to be rounded off, it shall be 
done in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 ‘Rules for rounding off numerical values (revised)’. 


IS 1448 [P : 54] : 2017 


Indian Standard 


METHODS OF TEST FOR PETROLEUM AND ITS 
PRODUCTS 
[P : 54] 


DETERMINATION OF PHOSPHORUS CONTENT — QUINOLINE 
PHOSPHOMOLYBDATE METHOD 


( Third Revision ) 


1 SCOPE 


1.1 This standard specifies quinoline 
phosphomolybdate method for the determination of 
phosphorus content of unused lubricating oil and 
additive concentrates. The method is applicable to 
products containing any of the phosphorus compounds 
in normal use and having phosphorus contents between 
0.005 and 10.0 percent (m/m). 


NOTE — There is no reason to doubt its applicability to filtered, 
used lubricating oils, but no systematic study of this application 
has been made. 


1.2 The methods is free from most interferences 
because the high insolubility of the quinoline 
phosphomolybdate precipitate leads to constant 
composition and freedom from most adsorbed or 
occluded impurities, especially from cations which 
would otherwise interfere in the subsequent titration 
of the precipitate. 

NOTE — Barium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, aluminium, 

alkali salts, citric acid and citrates, chromium up to 18 times 


the phosphorus content and titanium up to 3.5 times do not 
interfere with the method. 


2 REFERENCES 


The standards listed below contain provisions which, 
through reference in text, constitute provisions of this 
standard. At the time of publication, the editions 
indicated were valid. All standards are subject to 
revision, and parties to agreements based on this 
standard are encouraged to investigate the possibility 
of applying the most recent editions of the standards 
indicated below. 


IS No. Title 
1070 : 1992 Reagent grade water (third revision) 
1997 : 2008 Laboratory glassware — Burettes 


(third revision) 
3 PRINCIPLE 
A test portion of known mass is ignited with excess of 


zinc oxide, whereby phosphorus is converted to 
phosphate. The residue is dissolved in hydrochloric 


acid and any sulphide formed is oxidized with 
potassium bromate. Phosphorus is then precipitated as 
quinoline phosphomolybdate and determined 
volumetrically by addition of excess standard 
volumetric alkali solution and back-titration with 
standard volumetric acid solution. 


NOTE — Additive concentrates are diluted with phosphorus- 
free white oil to produce a working blend. 


4 REAGENTS AND MATERIALS 


4.1 Unless specified otherwise, pure chemicals and 
distilled water (see IS 1070) shall be employed in tests. 
During the analysis, use only reagents of recognized 
analytical grade. 


4.2 Zinc Oxide, finely divided. 
4.3 Potassium Bromate, solid. 


4.4 Hydrochloric Acid Solution (concentration 
= 1 mol/é). 


4.5 Hydrochloric Acid, concentrated solution, 
36 percent (m/m). 


4.6 Sodium Molybdate Solution — Dissolve 10 g of 
sodium hydroxide and 18 g of ammonia-free moly- 
bdenum trioxide in 200 ml of water and filter the solution. 


NOTE — To avoid high blanks caused by silicate interference, 
store the solution in a polyethylene container. 


4.7 Quinoline, redistilled synthetic or, if this is 
unobtainable, quinoline freshly distilled from the 
technical product. Collect the colourless distillate in 
the boiling range 232°C to 238°C. Store quinoline in a 
dark-coloured bottle and in the dark. 


4.8 Quinoline Solution — Dissolve 20 ml of the 
quinoline (see 4.7) in 800 ml of hot water acidified 
with 25 ml of the concentrated hydrochloric acid 
(see 4.5), add a little paper pulp (see note), shake well, 
cool, filter and dilute to 1 litre with water. This solution 
is stable for about 1 month. 


NOTE — Alternatively, a filter pad (see 5.6) may be dispersed 
in the solution. 


IS 1448 [P : 54] : 2017 


4.9 Hydrochloric Acid, standard volumetric solution, 
concentration = 0.1 mol/l, standardized to + 0.001 
mol/l. 


4.10 Sodium Hydroxide, standard volumetric 
solution, concentration = 0.1 mol/l, standardized to 
+ 0.001 mol/l. 


NOTE — To avoid high blanks caused by silicate interference, 
store the solution in a polyethylene container. 
4.11 Phenolphthalein, 1 g/l solution in 95 percent 
ethanol (v/v). 


4.12 Thymol Blue, 1 g/l solution in 95 percent ethanol 
(vW/). 


4.13 Mixed Indicator — Mix two volumes of 
phenolphthalein solution (see 4.11) with three volumes 
of thymol blue solution (see 4.12). 


4.14 Lead Acetate Test Paper 


4.15 Fluorescein Test Paper — Prepare by dipping 
a strip of filter paper into a 1 g/l solution of fluorescein, 
sodium salt, in 95 percent ethanol (v/v). 


4.16 White Oil, containing less than 0.005 percent 
(m/m) of phosphorus. 


5 APPARATUS 


5.1 Silica Crucibles, 40 m internal diameter at the 
top and 50 mm in height. The internal surface shall be 
smooth and free from pitting. 


5.2 Muffle Furnace, capable of maintaining a 
temperature of (700 + 25)°C, and fitted with ports to 
allow air circulation. 


5.3 Hot-Plate, heated by either electricity or steam, 
or boiling water-bath. 


5.4 Filtering Apparatus — A filter flask, of capacity 
500 ml, provided with a glass crucible adapter fitted 
in a rubber bung together with a rubber sleeve. 


5.5 Gooch Crucible, porcelain, 35 mm diameter at 
the top. 


5.6 Filter Pad, 20 mm diameter. 
5.7 Beakers, of capacity 25 and 500 ml. 
5.8 Conical flask, of capacity 500 ml. 


5.9 Burette, of capacity 50 ml graduated in 0.1 ml 
subdivisions, complying with the requirements 
of IS 1997. 


6 BLENDING PROCEDURE 


6.1 For samples having a phosphorus content greater 
than 0.3 percent (m/m), prepare a blend in the white 
oil (see 4.16) to give a phosphorus content in the range 
of 0.1 to 0.3 percent (m/m). 


6.2 Calculate the mass (m,), in grams, of the test 
portion for a 10 g blend, using the equation: 


m= 5 


where P is the approximate expected phosphorus 
content, expressed as a percentage by mass, of the test 
portion. 


Calculate the mass (m,), in grams, of white oil for an 
approximate 10 g blend using the equation. 


m,= 10m, 


6.3 Weigh, to the nearest 0.01 g, a test portion of mass 
(m,) into a 25 ml beaker (see 6.2). 


6.4 Weigh, to the nearest 0.01 g, a mass (m,) of white 
oil (see 6.2). 


6.5 Mix the test portion and white oil thoroughly be 
stirring and warming to approximately 50°C. 


7 PROCEDURE 


7.1 Test Portion 


The mass of test portion to be taken shall be estimated 
so that it contains not more than 3 mg of phosphorus 
(see Table 1). 


Table 1 Suggested Test Portion Size and Volume 
of Sodium Hydroxide Solution Required 


(Clause 7.1) 


Phosphorus Approximate Approximate Volume 
Content of Sample Mass of Test of Standard Sodium 
or Blend Portion Hydroxide Solution

D See 7.2.10 for use of sodium hydroxide. 


7.2 Determination 


7.2.1 For additive concentrates, weigh to the nearest 
0.001 g, 1 g of the homogenized blend (see 6.5) into a 
silica crucible (see 5.1). 


7.2.2 For lubricating oils, weigh to the nearest 0.001 
g, up to 3 g of the test portion into a silica crucible (see 
5.1). 


7.2.3 Cover the test portion with 8 g of the zinc oxide 
(see 4.2) and level the surface. Apply heat from a Meker 
burner to the surface until the zinc oxide becomes red 
hot, then, gently heat the crucible from below with a 


small Bunsen flame so that the oil burns off very gently. 
Finally, when no more vapour is evolved, ignite 
strongly and transfer to the muffle furnace (see 5.2), 
maintained at (700 + 25)°C, to burn off residual carbon. 


7.2.4 Allow the crucible to cool and carefully transfer 
its contents to a 500 ml beaker (see 5.7) (see note), 
completing the transfer with a jet of water from a wash- 
bottle. Add about 50 ml of water to the contents of the 
beaker and rinse the crucible with a few millilitres of 
the concentrated hydrochloric acid solution (see 4.5). 
Add the acid rinsing to the beaker and then add 
sufficient concentrated hydrochloric acid solution to 
bring the total volume of acid added to 23 ml. Heat the 
contents of the beaker until all the zinc oxide is 
dissolved, then boil the mixture until all hydrogen 
sulphide has been expelled from the solution [boil until 
the lead acetate test paper (see 4.14) is not coloured 
by the vapour]. 


NOTE — It is recommended that the dissolution of the zinc 
oxide be conducted under a fume hood with suitable extraction. 


7.2.5 Allow to cool slightly, add 30 to 50 mg of the 
potassium bromate (see 4.3) and boil the mixture until 
all free bromine has been expelled from the solution 
[boil until the fluorescein paper (see 4.15) is not 
discoloured by the vapour]. 

NOTE — Glass apparatus should have good resistance to alkali. 


Scratched or etched beakers should not be used for the 
precipitation of quinoline phosphomolybdate. 


7.2.6 Dilute the liquid to a volume of about 150 ml 
with water, add 30 ml of the concentrated hydrochloric 
acid solution (see 4.5) and 30 ml of the sodium 
molybdate solution (see 4.6), rinsing the sides of the 
beaker with a little water after each addition. Place the 
beaker on the hot-plate (see 5.3) and bring the liquid 
to the boil. Add a few drops of the quinoline solution 
(see 4.8) from a coarse tipped burette or pipette, 
swirling the liquid during the addition. Bring it to the 
boil again and add 2 ml of the quinoline solution drop 
by drop with swirling. To the gently boiling liquid, 
add the quinoline solution in 2 to 3 ml increments until 
a total of 25 ml has been added, swirling during the 
addition. Stand the beaker on the edge of the hot-plate 
or on the boiling water bath (see 5.3) for 15 min for 
the precipitate to settle. Allow it to cool to ambient 
temperature. 


7.2.7 Decant the clear supernatant liquid through the 
Gooch crucible (see 5.5), fitted with a filter pad (see 
5.6) with applied suction, and wash the precipitate 
twice by recantation with 20 ml portions of the 
hydrochloric acid solution (see 4.4). Transfer the 
precipitate to the filter pad with cold water and wash 
the beaker several times with volumes of 25 to 30 ml 
of water to free the beaker from acid. 


IS 1448 [P : 54] : 2017 


7.2.8 Use these washes also to wash the precipitate 
on the filter pad, allowing each portion of liquid to 
pass through before pouring on the next. Continue to 
wash until one portion of wash liquid fails to decolorize 
the solution when passed into a clean flask containing 
a few drops of phenolphthalein (see 4.11) and 1 drop 
of the standard sodium hydroxide solution (see 4.10). 
Six washes are usually sufficient. 


7.2.9 Transfer the precipitate and filter pad to the 
conical flask (see 5.8) with a glass rod with a drawn- 
out pointed end. Insert a glass funnel into the flask 
and wash into it any portions of the precipitate 
remaining in the Gooch crucible using carbon dioxide- 
free water. Remove any traces of precipitate adhering 
to the funnel by wiping with a slip of moist filter paper; 
add this to the contents of the flask. Add carbon 
dioxide-free water until the volume of liquid in the 
flask is about 120 ml. Shake the flask until the filter 
pad and filter paper are disintegrated and the precipitate 
is thoroughly dispersed. Ensure that no lumps re-main, 
otherwise difficulty may be encountered in dissolving 
them in the sodium hydroxide solution. 


7.2.10 From the burette, slowly add the standard 
volumetric sodium hydroxide solution (see 4.10), 
shaking the flask vigorously to ensure complete 
solution of the precipitate. Continue to add the sodium 
hydroxide solution until the precipitate has dissolved 
and add approximately 5 ml in excess. Use table | to 
estimate the volume of alkali required. Record the 
volume V, of the standard volumetric sodium 
hydroxide solution added. 


7.2.11 Add about six drops of the mixed indicator 
(see 4.13) and titrate with the standard volumetric 
hydrochloric acid solution (see 4.9) until the colour 
changes from violet through grey and suddenly to pale 
yellow. Record the volume V, of the standard 
volumetric hydrochloric acid solution used in the back- 
titration. 


7.2.12 Carry out a blank test in parallel following the 
same procedure and using the same quantities of the 
reagents [except the standard volumetric sodium 
hydroxide solution (see 4.10) and standard volumetric 
hydrochloric acid solution (see 4.9)], but omitting the 
test portion. In the final titration, add 5.0 ml of the 
standard volumetric, sodium hydroxide solution and 
titrate with the standard volumetric hydrochloric acid 
solution. Record this volume V3. 


8 EXPRESSION OF RESULTS 


8.1 Method of Calculation 


8.1.1 Calculate the phosphorus content P, expressed 
as a percentage by mass, of a blended sample, using 
the equation:

acid solution used for the back-titration, in 
ml; 

V, = volume of standard volumetric hydrochloric 
acid solution used for the blank test, in ml; 

my = mass of the blend taken for the 
determination, in g; 

m, = mass of original blend, in g; and 

m, = mass of white oil sample in the 10 g in the 


10 g blend, in g. 


NOTE — If the concentrations of the standard volumetric 
solutions used are not exactly as specified in the list of 
reagents and materials, appropriate corrections should be 
made. 


8.1.2 Calculate the phosphorus content P, expressed 
as percentage by mass, of an unblended sample, using 
the equation:

NOTE — If the concentrations of the standard volumetric

reagents and materials, appropriate corrections should be 
made. 


8.1.3 Report the results to the nearest 0.01 percent (m/ 
m) above 0.1 percent (m/m) and to the nearest 0.001 
percent (m/m) below 0.1 percent (m/m). 


8.2 Precision 


The precision of this method as obtained by statistical 
examination of inter-laboratory test results, is as 
follows. 


8.2.1 Repeatability 


The difference between successive test results, obtained 


by the same operator with the same apparatus under 
constant operating conditions on identical test material, 
would, in the long run, in the normal and correct 
operation of the test method, exceed the following 
values only in one case in twenty. 


Level of Result (x), percent 
0.005 to 0.079 
0.08 to 10 


Repeatability, percent 
0.032 (x + 0.04) 
0.0318 °°? 


where x is the average of the two results. 
NOTE — Precision is given in Table 2 for typical values of x. 
8.2.2 Reproducibility 


The difference between two single and independent 
results, obtained by different operators working in 
different laboratories on identical test material, would, 
in the long run, in the normal and correct operation of 
the test method, exceed the following values only in 
one case in twenty. 


Level of Result (x), Reproducibility, 
percent percent 
0.005 to 0.079 0.074 (x + 0.04) 
0.08 to 10 0.118 x°°°? 


where x is the average of the two results. 


NOTE — Precision is given in Table 2 for typical values of x.

9 TEST REPORT 


The test report shall contain at least the following 
information: 


a) the type and identification of the product 
tested; 


b) the result of the test; 


c) any deviation, by agreement or otherwise, 
from the procedure specified; and 


d) the date of the test.
